scenarios.expected: Records and permissions work, file hashes match, and required encrypted configuration is usable with the retained key. Missing/wrong keys or missing files are detected; a backup archive alone never counts as a successful restore.
scenarios.actual: Took the coherent backup exactly as the article describes from the populated instance: stopped app and worker with Postgres left running, dumped the database in custom format, archived the local file volume through the app service, recorded the source and image identities, listed both archives and wrote SHA256SUMS, then restarted the services and confirmed readiness. Restored it into a different empty target with its own project, port and volumes: verified the retained hashes on that host, confirmed the target database held zero public tables, imported with pg_restore --exit-on-error, extracted the file archive into the app volume, and started the target with the separately retained AUTH_SECRET and OPENLAW_SECRET_KEY. The restored instance passed every verification in the article: existing accounts signed in, all records were present, both original and later Document Versions downloaded with matching SHA-256 values, the Contributor kept exactly its earlier reach including the Confidential refusal, the restored encrypted relay delivered a real message to a controlled recipient, and a new upload processed. Both failure cases in the article were exercised: a wrong OPENLAW_SECRET_KEY left records readable while the saved relay was unusable and nothing was delivered, and the retained key restored it; and removing one stored blob left the Document listed while its download failed with HTTP 500, which re-extracting the retained file archive into the same isolated target repaired back to the recorded hash.

limitations: The backup and restore covered the bundled Postgres database and the local file volume; object-store snapshot tooling was not exercised in this pass.
The restored target's controlled recipient was an owned mail catcher reachable under the same name as the source deployment's.
Local TLS uses an isolated Caddy internal CA and does not certify public DNS or certificate issuance.
S3 and Azure operations use owned local compatible services and explicit disposable keys; no cloud identity credential-chain claim.
Provider guides remain on unmerged PR #783; real provider checks C42/C43 are still blocked and are not waived.
The user will proofread the assembled complete suite; no human proofreading or feature-owner sign-off is recorded.
